Base directory for this skill: /Users/nick/conductor/workspaces/durhack-proj/tripoli/.claude/skills/hq-review

# hq-review

Review in your own worktree or workspace, never in the author's. Prefer a reviewer from a
different vendor than the author (the PR's `agent:*` label).

1. Check out the PR: `gh pr checkout <PR>`.
2. Find the issue: `gh pr view <PR> --json title,labels,closingIssuesReferences`, then
   `gh issue view <N>`. Note the Acceptance criteria, Scope and Do not touch.
3. Read the diff: `gh pr diff <PR>`. Flag any file outside Scope or inside Do not touch.
4. Run `./hq check` and the issue's Verify steps.
5. If `command -v claude && command -v codex` succeeds, run `entire review`. It runs Claude Code
   and Codex reviewers plus a judge from the shared profile and posts to the trail. Otherwise
   review by hand against each acceptance criterion.
6. Write the verdict to `.context/review-<PR>.md`:
   - Verdict: pass or changes.
   - Each acceptance criterion: met or not met, with evidence.
   - Findings, blocking first: `file:line`, the problem, a suggested fix.
   - The tail of `./hq check`.
7. Post it: `gh pr review <PR> --comment --body-file .context/review-<PR>.md`.
   Use `--comment`: you cannot approve a PR opened from your own account.
8. Label it:
   - pass: `gh pr edit <PR> --add-label review:pass --remove-label review:changes`
   - changes: `gh pr edit <PR> --add-label review:changes --remove-label review:pass`
9. Do not push fixes to the author's branch and do not merge. Tell the human the verdict.

+import { describe, expect, test } from "bun:test";
+import { roadTrafficDisturbance } from "../domain";
+import sensorsFixture from "./fixtures/city-sensors.json";
+import { citySensors, sensorLevel } from "./sensors";
+
+describe("city sensor fixture", () => {
+  const sensors = citySensors.parse(sensorsFixture);
+
+  test("holds about ten Newcastle sensors, all indicative", () => {
+    expect(sensors).toHaveLength(10);
+    expect(sensors.every((s) => s.indicative)).toBe(true);
+    expect(new Set(sensors.map((s) => s.id)).size).toBe(sensors.length);
+  });
+
+  test("covers shaded, out-of-range and not-enough-data sensors", () => {
+    expect(sensors.some((s) => !s.notEnoughData && !s.outOfRange)).toBe(true);
+    expect(sensors.some((s) => s.outOfRange)).toBe(true);
+    expect(sensors.some((s) => s.notEnoughData)).toBe(true);
+  });
+
+  test("%HSD follows the WHO curve", () => {
+    for (const s of sensors) {
+      if (s.lnight30 === null) continue;
+      const expected = roadTrafficDisturbance(s.lnight30);
+      expect(s.pctHighlySleepDisturbed).toBeCloseTo(expected.percentHighlyDisturbed, 1);
+      expect(s.outOfRange).toBe(expected.outOfRange);
+    }
+  });
+
+  test("not enough data means fewer than 30 nights", () => {
+    for (const s of sensors) expect(s.notEnoughData).toBe(s.nights < 30);
+  });
+
+  test("rejects a non-indicative sensor and a missing estimate", () => {
+    expect(sensorLevel.safeParse({ ...sensors[0], indicative: false }).success).toBe(false);
+    expect(sensorLevel.safeParse({ ...sensors[0], lnight30: null }).success).toBe(false);
+  });
+});
diff --git a/packages/shared/src/city/sensors.ts b/packages/shared/src/city/sensors.ts
new file mode 100644

+++ b/packages/shared/src/city/sensors.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,38 @@
+import { z } from "zod";
+
+/**
+ * One Newcastle Urban Observatory noise sensor on the city map.
+ * Figures are an indicative road-traffic estimate, never a measured disturbance rate
+ * (`docs/DOMAIN.md`).
+ */
+export const sensorLevel = z
+  .object({
+    id: z.string().min(1),
+    name: z.string().min(1),
+    lat: z.number().min(-90).max(90),
+    lon: z.number().min(-180).max(180),
+    /** Energy average of nightly Lnight in dB; null when there is not enough data */
+    lnight30: z.number().nullable(),
+    /** Nights of data behind the estimate */
+    nights: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
+    /** Indicative % highly sleep disturbed from the WHO curve; null when there is not enough data */
+    pctHighlySleepDisturbed: z.number().nullable(),
+    /** Lnight fell outside 40 to 65 dB and was clamped for the estimate */
+    outOfRange: z.boolean(),
+    /** Fewer than 30 nights: show the sensor but don't shade it */
+    notEnoughData: z.boolean(),
+    indicative: z.literal(true),
+    /** ISO 8601 timestamp of the latest reading used */
+    updatedAt: z.iso.datetime(),
+  })
+  .refine((s) => !s.notEnoughData || (s.lnight30 === null && s.pctHighlySleepDisturbed === null), {
+    message: "a sensor without enough data has no Lnight or %HSD",
+  })
+  .refine((s) => s.notEnoughData || (s.lnight30 !== null && s.pctHighlySleepDisturbed !== null), {
+    message: "a sensor with enough data needs Lnight and %HSD",
+  });
+export type SensorLevel = z.infer<typeof sensorLevel>;
+
+/** Output of the city sensors query. */
+export const citySensors = z.array(sensorLevel);
+export type CitySensors = z.infer<typeof citySensors>;

=== 16
### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `spikes.ts`: rolling-median baseline and a threshold constant turn 1 Hz relative dB into spikes

301-into each new workspace via `.worktreeinclude`. For a plain git worktree, copy `.env` by hand.
302-
303-| Name | Used by | Where to get it |
304-|---|---|---|
305-| `MONGO_URI` | API, worker | MongoDB Atlas cluster (MLH credit) |
306-| `TIGER_URI` | API, worker | Tiger Cloud service |
307-| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | API | Google AI Studio, **paid tier** (enable billing in hour one) |
308-| `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | API | ElevenLabs (MLH promo code) |
309-| `SOLANA_RPC_URL`, `SOLANA_KEYPAIR` | API | Mainnet RPC; a small funded keypair used only for memos |
310-| `STREET_MANAGER_TOPIC_ARN` | API | Street Manager open data registration (register in hour one) |
311-| `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` | App | `https://<ip>.sslip.io`, or the local server in development. Not a secret |
312-| `VULTR_API_KEY` | Terraform | Vultr account (MLH credit) |
313-| `MONGODB_ATLAS_PUBLIC_KEY`, `MONGODB_ATLAS_PRIVATE_KEY` | Terraform | Atlas org API key |
314-| Tiger Cloud provider credentials | Terraform | Tiger Cloud console; names per the provider docs |
315-| `TF_VAR_admin_ip`, `TF_VAR_image`, `TF_VAR_registry_user`, `TF_VAR_registry_password`, `TF_VAR_mongo_uri`, `TF_VAR_tiger_uri`, `TF_VAR_app_env` | Terraform | See `infra/terraform.tfvars.example`; `app_env` carries the API keys above to the server |
316-
317-Only `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` variables reach the app, and they end up in the bundle: never put a key there.
318-
319-## Deploy
320-Either of us deploys. The demo runs from tag `demo-v1`.
321-- `infra/` holds Terraform: SSH key, private container registry, firewall (22 from `admin_ip`
322-  only; 80 and 443 open for Caddy), a `vc2-2c-4gb` Ubuntu 24.04 instance in `lhr`, and the Atlas IP
323-  access list for the instance's IP. Keys come from variables, never the repo.
324-- The `Dockerfile` builds the server and `expo export --platform web` into one image; the API
325-  serves the web build on port 8080 (`docker run -p 8080:8080 kip`). Without database URIs it
326-  still boots, serving `/health`, the web build and the stubs. Steps: `infra/README.md`.
327-- cloud-init installs Docker, writes `/opt/kip/.env`, a Caddyfile and a compose file, derives an
328-  `<ip>.sslip.io` hostname from instance metadata, logs in to the registry, then runs the API,
329-  the worker (same image, `main.worker.ts`) and Caddy.
330-- Ship a new image: `docker build -t <image> . && docker push <image>`, then on the server
331-  `cd /opt/kip && docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`.
332-- The API retries its database connections on boot, because the Atlas access list is applied
333-  after the instance exists. It then applies pending Tiger migrations and Mongo indexes.
334-- The iOS app is a dev-client build installed on the demo phone; it is not deployed by Terraform.
335-- Demo: `terraform apply -replace=vultr_instance.api` rebuilds only the server; data stays put.
336-- To confirm against provider docs before relying on them: the Vultr region and the registry
337-  plan. The image reference and registry credentials are variables, so nothing depends on the
338-  registry's `urn` attribute.

content.thinking: Terraform authenticates with an Atlas org API key to add the instance IP to the project's IP access list. I need to check the infra config to see which resources are involved.

input.command: rg -n -i "mongodbatlas" infra | head -20

content.text:
Give it **Project Owner** on the project that holds your cluster. Add it at Organization → Access Manager → API Keys.

Terraform only uses the key for one thing, `mongodbatlas_project_ip_access_list.api` (`infra/main.tf:66`). That adds the Vultr instance's IP to the cluster's access list. It doesn't create clusters or users.

- **Project IP Access List:** the key must be added to the project. Org-level keys don't reach projects until you add them.
- **Role:** the lowest role that can edit the IP access list is **Project Owner**. I believe Project Read Only and Project Data Access roles can't, so check this against Atlas's role table.
- **Org role:** the key's org role can stay at Organization Member, since only the project role matters.
- **Key access list:** when you create the key, Atlas asks for an API access list. Add your own IP, or the Terraform run from your laptop will be rejected.

The key has a public half and a private half, and the private half is shown only once. Put them in `.env` as `MONGODB_ATLAS_PUBLIC_KEY` and `MONGODB_ATLAS_PRIVATE_KEY`.

The app's own connection (`MONGO_URI`) uses a separate database user, not this key. Create that under Database Access with read and write on the Kip database.

**Where Cloudflare does fit**
- **Cloudflare Tunnel (free):** run the same Docker image on your own machine and expose it at a public HTTPS hostname. That replaces Vultr, Caddy and `sslip.io`, and it's free with no card. The downside is that the demo then depends on your laptop and venue Wi-Fi. A backup video (#80) covers that.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing which kind of tunnel to explain. A quick trycloudflare tunnel needs no account, while a named tunnel needs a Cloudflare account and a domain on Cloudflare for a custom hostname. A free quick tunnel is started with a single cloudflared command that gives a random *.trycloudflare.com address.

Next I'm checking the access rules: the Atlas IP access list needs my laptop's IP, or 0.0.0.0/0 to allow anything. The phone's app bakes the API URL into its bundle, so a quick tunnel that changes each run would force a rebuild, which makes a stable hostname matter for the demo.

content.text:
It depends on whether you need a stable URL. I'm going from memory on how Cloudflare Tunnel works.

**Quick tunnel: nothing at all.**
- Install `cloudflared` with `brew install cloudflared`.
- Run `cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080`, since the API serves on port 8080.
- It prints a random `https://<words>.trycloudflare.com` address. There's no account and no domain.
- The address changes every run, and it has no uptime guarantee. The app reads `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` at build time, so every new address means a rebuild of the dev client. The demo phone needs a fixed one.

**Named tunnel: a stable address.**
- A free Cloudflare account.
- A domain whose DNS is on Cloudflare. A free tunnel hostname needs one. Buying a domain is cheap, but not free, and you may get one free through a student pack or MLH.
- Create the tunnel in the Zero Trust dashboard (free plan), then copy its token into `.env` and run `cloudflared tunnel run --token <token>`.
- Point a hostname such as `kip.yourdomain.com` at `http://localhost:8080`. Set `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` to that address once.

**Also needed either way**
- **MongoDB Atlas:** add your laptop's IP to the cluster's access list, or Atlas rejects the connection. At a venue your IP changes, so you may have to open it to `0.0.0.0/0` for the weekend.
- **`.env`:** the same `.env` as the server, with the API's `docker run -p 8080:8080 kip` or `bun` start command running locally.
- **Wi-Fi:** the phone and the laptop both need internet, but the tunnel means they don't have to be on the same network.

If you have no domain, use the quick tunnel for development and treat the stable-URL problem as the reason to keep Vultr for the demo.

No API key. Cloudflare Tunnel doesn't use one for this.

- **Quick tunnel:** no credentials at all. You run one command and get a URL.
- **Named tunnel:** it uses a **tunnel token**. You get it from the Cloudflare dashboard when you create the tunnel and pass it to `cloudflared tunnel run --token ...`. It acts like a secret, so put it in `.env` and keep it out of git and out of chat. You also need the free account and a domain on Cloudflare.

Terraform and an API token would only come into it if we automated the Cloudflare setup, which I wouldn't do here, since the dashboard takes a couple of minutes.

content.text:
Tailscale fits better than Cloudflare here, because it gives a stable HTTPS address with no domain. I'm going from memory, so check the current docs.

**What you need**
- A free Tailscale account (the Personal plan), with Tailscale installed on the laptop and signed in.
- In the admin console: turn on **MagicDNS** and **HTTPS certificates**, and allow **Funnel** for the machine.
- No API key. Sign-in is the only credential.

**Two ways to use it**
- **`tailscale serve` (private):** `tailscale serve --bg 8080` publishes the API at `https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net`, but only to devices on your tailnet. The demo iPhone would need the Tailscale app, signed in to the same account. It's private and good for development.
- **`tailscale funnel` (public):** `tailscale funnel --bg 8080` makes the same address reachable from the open internet. Judges' devices and the web dashboard need this, because they aren't on your tailnet. Funnel only allows ports 443, 8443 and 10000, and has bandwidth limits that Tailscale doesn't publish.

**Compared with Cloudflare Tunnel**
- The address is stable and free, with no domain to buy.
- The `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` can be set once, to the `ts.net` hostname.
- The same limits apply: the demo runs from your laptop, Atlas needs your IP in its access list (or `0.0.0.0/0`), and the laptop must stay awake and online.

I'd use `serve` to develop, switch to `funnel` for the demo, and keep the backup video for when the laptop or Wi-Fi fails.

# Hack brief

Event facts, deadlines and prize targets. Fill in the TBDs at kick-off.

## Event
- DurHack 2026, an MLH member event. About 24 hours.
- Dates: TBD. Plan assumes 24 hours from about 10am, so hours 14 to 20 fall overnight.
- Team: Ellis and Nick. Both of us own everything; lanes in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` only split
  work between agents.
- Project: **Kip**, sleep, noise and the city. See `docs/SPEC.md` and `docs/BUSINESS.md`.
- MLH workshop: Intro to Google AI Studio (time announced at the opening ceremony).

## Deadlines
| What | When |
|---|---|
| Kick-off (hacking starts) | TBD |
| M0 skeleton merged and deployed | kick-off + ~2h |
| Checkpoint: Watch works, else phone only | kick-off + 2h |
| Checkpoint: one full night stored end to end | kick-off + 14h |
| Code freeze (judging minus 3h), tag `demo-v1` | TBD (plan: kick-off + 20h) |
| Submission (Devpost) | TBD |
| Judging | TBD |

## Theme
TBD.
Mapbox attribution stays visible.
**Consequences:** The web export shows Newcastle tiles only when the public token is set. A missing
token shows a message naming `EXPO_PUBLIC_MAPBOX_TOKEN` instead of a blank map. The phone build does
not gain a Mapbox native SDK. Secret Mapbox tokens (`sk.`) stay out of the app.

## 2026-11-14: Open questions answered: no home sensor, one sponsor track
**Context:** Two open questions in `docs/SPEC.md` changed the plan. The human answered both.
**Decision:** Nobody sleeps at home in Newcastle near an Observatory noise sensor during the event,
so the city map uses sensors near the venue and demo step 4 uses a night exported from HealthKit
(the SPEC's stated fallback). Each team is limited to one sponsor track, so we enter MongoDB per
"Tiger for time series, MongoDB for documents and geo". Still open: the event length and start
time, and what the "35" in the team's notes means. Both keep their assumptions in `docs/SPEC.md`.
**Consequences:** Follow the MongoDB fallback in that entry. Do not build on the "35".

content.text:
**Writing needs a keypair, and reading doesn't.**

- **Writing a memo** is a transaction, so something must sign it and pay the fee. That is the keypair in `SOLANA_KEYPAIR`. It's the fee payer in `apps/server/src/integrations/solana.ts`, and there's no way around it on any Solana network.
- **Reading a memo back** (`readMemo(signature)`) needs only the RPC URL, no wallet. So the council's tamper check can verify a log with no keypair, using only the signature.

**Ways to avoid spending real money**
- **Devnet (free):** the free faucet at faucet.solana.com gives devnet SOL. The code already takes any RPC URL, so you'd point `SOLANA_RPC_URL` at a devnet endpoint and fund the keypair for free. The catch is that the project says mainnet (`docs/DECISIONS.md:89`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:80`). The pitch is that a council can check it without trusting Kip, which needs a public chain. Devnet is wiped and has no standing, so judges would see it as a demo. It's fine for development, but I'd switch to mainnet for the demo.
- **Skip the chain:** leave Solana out and show only the local hash check. That drops the Best Use of Solana entry (`docs/hack/BRIEF.md:36`, which is marked "weakest fit" anyway) and the "tamper check" demo step (`docs/SPEC.md`, step 6). #71, #72 and #73 would need rescoping.

**Recommendation.** Use a devnet keypair now. You can run the verification step today at no cost, and the keypair format is the same. Before the demo, make a mainnet keypair and spend the few pence. A memo costs a fraction of a penny, so £2 lasts the whole event.

I can run the check against devnet if you add a devnet `SOLANA_RPC_URL` and fund the keypair. I'd use a separate variable for that run, so I don't change your mainnet one.

    Serve Kip at kip.edenmatrix.xyz through a Cloudflare tunnel (#151) (#153)
    
    * Serve Kip at kip.edenmatrix.xyz through a Cloudflare tunnel
    
    The API, the worker and Kip's own cloudflared run as one compose project on the shared Docker host, with no published ports: the tunnel is the only way in. The image is built on the host from the committed tree, so there is no registry, and every setting stays in the host's .env. The tunnel token and its hostname route live in Zero Trust, not in the repo.
    
    Each container gets only the variables it reads. A bare name in the compose environment takes its value from --env-file, so a setting missing there stays unset instead of arriving as an empty string, which one Gemini setting would read as zero.
    
    - compose.yml: api and worker from kip/server:live, never pulled, with a health check long enough to cover the database retries on boot. The worker waits for a healthy API, because the API applies the migrations its jobs write to.
    - compose.tunnel.yml: cloudflared as an override, pinned to the version the host's other stacks run, non-root and read-only, holding only the tunnel token.
    - deploy.sh: ships a commit over ssh, runs the remote half, then checks /health through Cloudflare.
    - remote-deploy.sh: builds and retags the image, installs the compose files, waits for the stack, checks /health and the web build from inside the API container, and keeps the previous build for rollback.
    - tests: none for deploy scripts; the smoke step fails the deploy when /health or the web build does not answer.
    
    Entire-Checkpoint: 22d9cebfdc15
    
    * Keep the tunnel compose file in Biome's YAML format
    
    Biome formats YAML too, so the comment on the shared logging settings moves above its key and the lint check passes.
    
    - compose.yml: the logging comment sits above x-logging instead of inside the mapping.
